lesson.title: The Jazz Age: America Dances to a New Rhythm
lesson.summary: The 1920s earned the nickname the Jazz Age as a new musical style born in Black communities swept the nation, symbolizing a broader cultural shift toward youthful rebellion, changing gender norms, and restless modern living.
lesson.body:
The writer F. Scott Fitzgerald gave the decade its enduring nickname, describing it as the Jazz Age in his fiction and later in a 1931 essay looking back on the era. Jazz music itself had developed earlier, in Black communities in New Orleans, blending blues, ragtime, and improvisational performance into something entirely new. As the Great Migration carried Black musicians north to cities like Chicago and New York, jazz traveled with them, and Harlem became one of its most important national centers, closely tied to the broader literary and artistic energy of the Harlem Renaissance happening in the same neighborhood at the same time. Musicians like Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington, along with blues singers such as Bessie Smith, turned jazz into the most popular and influential American music of the decade.

Jazz did not stay confined to Black neighborhoods or Southern origins. The same consumer technologies reshaping the rest of American life, phonograph records and especially radio, carried jazz recordings into white middle class homes across the country, turning a regional Black art form into a genuinely national craze. Dance halls filled with young people doing the Charleston and other new dances built around jazz rhythms. This musical explosion became shorthand for a broader set of social changes: women who called themselves flappers cut their hair short, wore shorter skirts, smoked in public, and generally rejected the more restrictive social expectations placed on their mothers' generation.

Not everyone welcomed the change. Many older and more conservative Americans viewed jazz music, flapper fashion, and the loosening of traditional courtship and behavior as signs of moral decline, and this generational and cultural conflict ran through much of the decade's politics and popular commentary. The tension only deepened because so much of this new youth culture unfolded in an illegal setting, the speakeasy, a hidden bar where jazz, dancing, and alcohol mixed freely in open defiance of the law that had just made drinking illegal nationwide.
